items.descriptionOriginal: Η εικόνα του ιδιοφυούς, αλλά βασανισμένου καλλιτέχνη έχει αφήσει έντονο αποτύπωμα στη συλλογική φαντασία. Ζωγράφοι, συγγραφείς και μουσικοί που δημιούργησαν σπουδαία έργα, ενώ παράλληλα αντιμετώπιζαν ψυχικές δυσκολίες, έχουν τροφοδοτήσει επί δεκαετίες την πεποίθηση ότι δημιουργικότητα και ψυχική ευαλωτότητα συνδέονται στενά . Ισχύει, όμως, κάτι τέτοιο; Μια νέα μελέτη, που δημοσιεύθηκε στο Molecular Psychiatry , επιχείρησε να «φωτίσει» αυτή τη σύνθετη σχέση. Τα ευρήματα των ερευνητών από το Ινστιτούτο Max Planck Εμπειρικής Αισθητικής, το Karolinska Institutet και άλλα επιστημονικά ιδρύματα αποκαλύπτουν ενδιαφέρουσες διαφορές. Μια καθιερωμένη πεποίθηση Σύμφωνα με τη Miriam A. Mosing, επικεφαλής της νέας μελέτης, η ιδέα ότι η ιδιοφυΐα και η ψυχική ασθένεια συμβαδίζουν έχει βαθιές ρίζες, ιδιαίτερα στον χώρο της τέχνης. Ωστόσο, τα επιστημονικά στοιχεία που υποστηρίζουν αυτή την αντίληψη είναι ασυνεπή. Η ερευνητική ομάδα αξιοποίησε δεδομένα από δύο έρευνες που πραγματοποιήθηκαν στη Σουηδία, κατά τις περιόδους 2012-2013 και 2022-2023. Συνολικά, συμμετείχαν 14.658 δίδυμοι, ενώ 6.419 απ’ αυτούς έλαβαν μέρος και στις δύο φάσεις, επιτρέποντας στους επιστήμονες να εξετάσουν πιθανές μεταβολές μέσα στον χρόνο. Οι συμμετέχοντες απάντησαν σε ερωτήσεις σχετικά με τα επιτεύγματά τους σε διαφορετικούς δημιουργικούς τομείς, όπως η μουσική , η συγγραφή , ο χορός , το θέατρο και οι εικαστικές τέχνες , αλλά και η επιστήμη και οι εφευρέσεις . Παράλληλα, καταγράφηκαν πληροφορίες για το επάγγελμα, την προσωπικότητα και την ψυχική τους υγεία. Οι ερευνητές εξέτασαν τόσο τα ψυχικά συμπτώματα που ανέφεραν οι ίδιοι οι συμμετέχοντες, όσο και καταγεγραμμένες ψυχιατρικές διαγνώσεις, μεταξύ των οποίων η μείζων καταθλιπτική και η διπολική διαταραχή . Σε δεύτερη φάση, αξιολογήθηκε επίσης η αποκλίνουσα σκέψη , δηλαδή η ικανότητα ενός ανθρώπου να παράγει διαφορετικές ιδέες ή πιθανές λύσεις σ’ ένα πρόβλημα. Καλλιτεχνική και επιστημονική δημιουργικότητα: Μια σημαντική διαφορά Τα αποτελέσματα έδειξαν ότι οι άνθρωποι με υψηλότερη καλλιτεχνική δημιουργικότητα παρουσίαζαν, κατά μέσο όρο, περισσότερες δυσκολίες ψυχικής υγείας. Η εικόνα, ωστόσο, ήταν διαφορετική στην περίπτωση της επιστημονικής δημιουργικότητας. Οι επιδόσεις και τα επιτεύγματα στους επιστημονικούς τομείς δε συνδέθηκαν σημαντικά με ψυχικές δυσκολίες. Μάλιστα, ορισμένοι δείκτες επιστημονικής δημιουργικότητας συσχετίστηκαν με λιγότερα προβλήματα ψυχικής υγείας . Τα ευρήματα δεν υποδηλώνουν ότι η τέχνη προκαλεί ψυχικές διαταραχές, ούτε ότι οι καλλιτέχνες αντιμετωπίζουν αναπόφευκτα περισσότερα προβλήματα ψυχικής υγείας. Η μελέτη καταγράφει απλώς στατιστικές συσχετίσεις. Τι ρόλο παίζουν τα γονίδια; Το γεγονός ότι η έρευνα βασίστηκε σε δεδομένα διδύμων επέτρεψε στους επιστήμονες να διερευνήσουν σε ποιον βαθμό οι παρατηρούμενες συσχετίσεις επηρεάζονται από κοινούς γενετικούς και περιβαλλοντικούς παράγοντες. Οι αναλύσεις έδειξαν ότι οι γενετικές επιδράσεις συμβάλλουν, πράγματι, στη σχέση ανάμεσα στην καλλιτεχνική δημιουργικότητα και τις ψυχικές δυσκολίες. «Η υψηλότερη καλλιτεχνική δημιουργικότητα συνδέθηκε με περισσότερα προβλήματα ψυχικής υγείας και τα γονίδια φαίνεται να παίζουν σημαντικό ρόλο σ’ αυτή τη συσχέτιση», επιβεβαίωσε ο Penghao Xia, πρώτος συγγραφέας της μελέτης. Αυτό, ωστόσο, δεν υποβαθμίζει τη σημασία του περιβάλλοντος – χρειάζεται περαιτέρω έρευνα για να αποσαφηνιστεί πώς αλληλεπιδρούν η γενετική προδιάθεση, οι εμπειρίες ζωής και άλλοι παράγοντες. Οι ερευνητές κατέληξαν σε ένα ακόμη ενδιαφέρον συμπέρασμα: Άτομα που είχαν εμφανίσει περισσότερα καταθλιπτικά συμπτώματα στο παρελθόν έτειναν να παρουσιάζουν αργότερα μεγαλύτερη δεκτικότητα σε νέες εμπειρίες – ένα χαρακτηριστικό προσωπικότητας που συνδέεται με την περιέργεια, τη φαντασία και την προθυμία εξερεύνησης νέων ιδεών. Οι ερευνητές διευκρινίζουν: Το εύρημα δε σημαίνει ότι η κατάθλιψη ενισχύει τη δημιουργικότητα ή ότι οι ψυχικές δυσκολίες αποτελούν προϋπόθεση καλλιτεχνικής έκφρασης. Τελικά, η δημιουργικότητα είναι «συνδεδεμένη» με την ψυχική ευαλωτότητα; Σύμφωνα με τα νέα ευρήματα, η απάντηση δε φαίνεται να είναι τόσο απλή όσο υποδηλώνει το στερεότυπο του «βασανισμένου καλλιτέχνη». Η δημιουργικότητα δεν αποτελεί ένα ενιαίο χαρακτηριστικό και η σχέση της με την ψυχική υγεία διαφέρει ανάλογα με τον τρόπο που εκφράζεται και μετριέται. Επόμενος στόχος των ερευνητών είναι να κατανοήσουν καλύτερα ποιοι γενετικοί μηχανισμοί μπορεί να βρίσκονται πίσω από τη συσχέτιση της καλλιτεχνικής δημιουργικότητας με την ψυχική υγεία. Το σημαντικότερο συμπέρασμα, πάντως, είναι ότι η καλλιτεχνική δημιουργικότητα και οι ψυχικές δυσκολίες μπορεί να μοιράζονται κοινό «έδαφος», χωρίς η μία να αποτελεί απαραίτητη προϋπόθεση ή αιτία της άλλης. Με άλλα λόγια, δε χρειάζεται να υποφέρει κανείς για να δημιουργεί. Η δημιουργικότητα, σε οποιαδήποτε μορφή της, δεν πρέπει να αντιμετωπίζεται ως ένδειξη ψυχικής διαταραχής. Διαβάστε επίσης Είμαστε πιο δημιουργικοί το πρωί; Έρευνα απαντά Δημιουργικότητα: Γιατί «γεννάμε» ιδέες όταν περπατάμε Τι συμβαίνει στο μυαλό των δημιουργικών ανθρώπων – Γιατί δεν χρειάζονται οθόνες

items.description: Μια ειδική λευκή βαφή που αναπτύχθηκε στο Πανεπιστήμιο της Νότιας Φλόριντα θα μπορούσε να προσφέρει έναν νέο τρόπο για την ψύξη των κτιρίων, τη μείωση της κατανάλωσης ενέργειας και τη μείωση της εξάρτησης από τον κλιματισμό. items.descriptionOriginal: Δέκα λεπτά περπάτημα αμέσως μετά το γεύμα μπορούν να συγκρατήσουν την απότομη άνοδο του σακχάρου αποτελεσματικότερα από έναν τριπλάσιο σε διάρκεια περίπατο που ξεκινά μισή ώρα αργότερα. Αυτό δείχνει μελέτη του Πανεπιστημίου Ritsumeikan στην Ιαπωνία, η οποία επανέρχεται στο προσκήνιο καθώς συνεχίζεται η συζήτηση για το αν η πρωινή ή η βραδινή βάδιση ωφελεί καλύτερα τον γλυκαιμικό έλεγχο. Η απάντηση των ειδικών είναι ότι καμία από τις δύο επιλογές δεν υπερέχει απόλυτα. Η πρωινή κίνηση αντισταθμίζει την ορμονικά προκαλούμενη αύξηση της γλυκόζης στο ξύπνημα, ενώ η βραδινή περιορίζει τις αιχμές μετά το δείπνο. Γιατί έχει σημασία το πότε Στη δοκιμή, που δημοσιεύθηκε στο Scientific Reports, συμμετείχαν 12 υγιείς νέοι ενήλικες. Μετά από διάλυμα 75 γραμμαρίων γλυκόζης, καθένας πέρασε με τυχαία σειρά από τρεις συνθήκες : παρέμεινε καθιστός, περπάτησε δέκα λεπτά αμέσως ή βάδισε επί μισή ώρα, ξεκινώντας 30 λεπτά αργότερα. Οι μετρήσεις γίνονταν ανά δεκάλεπτο, για δύο ώρες. Και οι δύο περίπατοι μείωσαν τη συνολική έκθεση στη γλυκόζη σε σχέση με την ανάπαυση. Μόνο το άμεσο δεκάλεπτο , ωστόσο, συγκράτησε σημαντικά την κορυφή , στα 164,3 mg/dL έναντι 181,9 mg/dL. Η καθυστερημένη βάδιση έφτασε τα 175,8 mg/dL, διαφορά που δεν χαρακτηρίστηκε στατιστικά σημαντική. Ο επικεφαλής ερευνητής Kaito Hashimoto σημειώνει ότι ακόμη και ένας σύντομος περίπατος χωρίς καθυστέρηση μετά το γεύμα φάνηκε να αποδίδει, με όφελος παρόμοιο με εκείνο της μισάωρης βάδισης. Η εξήγηση, κατά τους συγγραφείς, είναι ότι η κίνηση προλαμβάνει την άνοδο που κορυφώνεται συνήθως 30 έως 60 λεπτά μετά το φαγητό, καθώς οι μύες που συσπώνται αντλούν γλυκόζη από το αίμα. Ωστόσο, τονίζουν ότι τα ευρήματα αφορούν προς το παρόν υγιείς νέους και χρειάζεται να επιβεβαιωθούν τόσο σε μεγαλύτερες ηλικίες όσο και σε άτομα με διαβήτη. Το πρωί και το «φαινόμενο της αυγής» Τις πρώτες πρωινές ώρες, το σάκχαρο τείνει να αυξάνεται ακόμη και μετά από ολονύχτια νηστεία. Το λεγόμενο «φαινόμενο της αυγής» (dawn phenomenon) οφείλεται σε ορμόνες, όπως η κορτιζόλη , που ωθούν το ήπαρ να απελευθερώσει γλυκόζη ενόψει της αφύπνισης. Στον διαβήτη τύπου 2 , η ινσουλίνη συχνά δεν αρκεί για να εξουδετερώσει αυτή την άνοδο. Σε παλαιότερη εργασία στο BioMed Research International , 20 ασθενείς με την πάθηση έκαναν 30 λεπτά μέτριας αερόβιας άσκησης σε διάδρομο πριν από το πρωινό. Η πρωινή αύξηση της γλυκόζης περιορίστηκε και ο έλεγχος βελτιώθηκε σε όλη την ημέρα. Αξίζει, βέβαια, να σημειωθεί ότι η έρευνα ήταν μικρή και δεν είχε ομάδα σύγκρισης. Τι χρειάζεται προσοχή το βράδυ Ο περίπατος μετά το δείπνο έχει ιδιαίτερη αξία για όσους καταναλώνουν τότε το πιο πλούσιο σε υδατάνθρακες γεύμα της ημέρας. Οι ειδικοί προειδοποιούν, όμως, ότι η έντονη δραστηριότητα λίγο πριν από τον ύπνο μπορεί να διαταράξει την ξεκούραση. Για όσους έχουν διαβήτη τύπου 1 ή χρησιμοποιούν ινσουλίνη, η άσκηση αργά το απόγευμα ή το βράδυ αυξάνει την πιθανότητα νυχτερινής υπογλυκαιμίας, δηλαδή επικίνδυνης πτώσης της γλυκόζης όσο κοιμόμαστε. Σε αυτές τις περιπτώσεις, οι αλλαγές στο πρόγραμμα άσκησης χρειάζεται να συζητούνται με τον θεράποντα ιατρό. Η καταλληλότερη στιγμή εξαρτάται από το πότε ανεβαίνει το σάκχαρο, τη φαρμακευτική αγωγή και τη ρουτίνα του καθενός. Όποιος καταγράφει υψηλές τιμές το πρωί μπορεί να επωφεληθεί από βάδιση πριν από το πρόγευμα, ενώ όποιος παρατηρεί αυξήσεις μετά το δείπνο, από έναν σύντομο περίπατο μετά το φαγητό. Σε κάθε περίπτωση, οι ειδικοί συμφωνούν ότι η τακτική κίνηση έχει μεγαλύτερη βαρύτητα από το ακριβές ωράριο. items.titleOriginal: A Hyderabad Stay-at-Home Dad Shares What It’s Really Like to Be a Full-Time Parent

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News The Many Ways Student-Led Climate Action Can Look Reading Time: 3 minutes Three Canadian schools doing three completely different projects, all with one common thread. By now, we can see that climate action doesn’t take just one shape. There are so many climate solutions that exist in this world, and it is particularly through the creativity and audacity of youth that we can implement them in the epicentres of community: schools. Sometimes, it’s a bike event that nearly 200 people show up to, or a compost bin that accidentally became a garden over summer break, or a dusty shed that a shop class turned into a net-zero community hub. Across three schools in the Canadian provinces of Newfoundland & Labrador, Ontario, and Prince Edward Island, students have been building, growing, and pedalling their way toward a greener school and pulling their communities along for the ride. Most students at École St. Matthew’s in St. John’s, Newfoundland live within two kilometres of their school, yet most arrive by car anyway. The school set out to change that habit with its annual spring community event: Bikefest. Their annual community cycling Bikefest, held in May, drew 164 registered participants (double last year’s 82), plus walk-ins that pushed the total close to 200. Their local Member of Parliament and the provincial Minister of Education both attended, and 15 children were matched with refurbished bikes and scooters and given helmets through a re-CYCLING initiative the school plans to expand next year. Additionally, one of Canada’s most prominent youth climate action journals, The Starfish Canada , even interviewed and published a piece on the project a few months later. Behind the event is a longer project that has installed bike racks, a repair station, and solar lighting at the school, while hosting safety courses and family cycling days. Student lead Sawyer wrote letters to local businesses asking for helmet discounts and volunteer support, and he received more responses than the emails his teacher sent. The city is starting to notice, too! “The city’s starting to see that shared use pathways are an opportunity,” said teacher lead Mr. Shoemaker. “We can get people walking. We can get people more healthy.” This next project started during lockdown, when a group of friends attending Eden High School in Ontario discovered they liked plants. When school returned in person, they formed a greenhouse club, only to find their school’s greenhouse had sat unused for decades, overtaken by overgrown plants and falling into disrepair. They cleared it out, researched how to repair it, and got to work. A student at Eden High School tends to their plants in their school’s greenhouse. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . The greenhouse is now fully functional, sealed against winter heat loss and actively used by students learning sustainable agriculture. A composting program ran successfully alongside it until the compost bin spontaneously became a volunteer garden over the summer, which is honestly a great problem to have. More recently, the school received a Go Wild grant from WWF Canada to build a wildflower pollinator garden beside the greenhouse. What began as a club fixing a broken structure has grown into a broader ecological vision for the school. “In a way, this project has launched our school into somewhat of a larger eco project,” said teacher lead Mike Idzenga. A Grade 9 student put it simply: “With all the tips and tricks that I learned this year, for the rest of my life I can do that to plant my own garden.” Three Oaks High School doesn’t shy away from hosting events: sports games, races, community presentations. When they finally built a new outdoor sports field, it came with an awkward problem: it was far from the kitchen where food for events was prepared. The TOSH Cares Club and shop program decided to fix it by using the unused shed sitting on school property. Students gather at Three Oaks High School to retrofit their multipurpose outbuilding. Photo courtesy of N:OW for Net-Zero . Students across programs retrofitted the building, insulating it, wiring a solar system, and turning it into a net-zero multipurpose outbuilding that can now host classes, clubs, and events. Many TOSH Cares students had never taken shop before, and many shop students had never engaged with environmental education. The project brought them together, and both groups left changed. A sign on the shed now describes its net-zero impact to anyone who walks by. Gabby Cierra, a Grade 12 student, said something worth sitting with: “It kinda feels like we almost can’t make as much of an impact because we are not old enough to start big programs… but I think this is an example that we can.” All three of these schools came to N:OW for Net-Zero , a pan-Canadian student-led climate action program, with a real, tangible wish to improve their school grounds and, ultimately, enhance the living conditions of those attending and surrounding them. If this isn’t proof that climate action looks like whatever young people decide to make it, then we don’t know what is! The post The Many Ways Student-Led Climate Action Can Look appeared first on Happy Eco News .

items.descriptionOriginal: Note: A trip to the hills can offer a welcome change from the haze, traffic, and polluted air of a busy city. But while a few days amid greener surroundings may give you a breather, travelling cannot be a permanent solution to the problem of air pollution. Hill towns, too, experience changing air quality, and their clean-air promise should never be taken for granted. If you are planning a getaway, however, these five hill stations are worth considering. Just remember to check their latest AQI before you set off. As winter approaches, the skies above several cities begin to look different. A familiar haze settles over buildings, traffic moves beneath a blanket of smog, and stepping outdoors becomes uncomfortable. For people living in crowded urban centres, even a morning walk can mean spending time in polluted air. It is little surprise that the hills begin to look inviting at this time of the year. With forest trails, open landscapes, and fewer vehicles than in major cities, mountain towns offer a different environment . But does travelling to the hills actually mean breathing cleaner air? Not necessarily. Tourism, road construction, traffic, and seasonal weather conditions can affect air quality even in smaller hill towns. Looking at local AQI readings, rather than assuming that every green destination has clean air, can help travellers make a more informed choice. Here are five hill destinations to consider, along with their latest available air quality readings. 1. Landour, Uttarakhand For Delhi residents looking for a mountain escape, Landour offers a suitable alternative to the crowded streets of Mussoorie. Situated above the popular hill station, this small cantonment town is surrounded by oak and deodar forests, with walking trails and old colonial-era buildings. For Delhi residents looking for a mountain escape, Landour offers a suitable alternative to the crowded streets of Mussoorie. Photograph: (Hire A Camp) Visitors can explore the Circular Road, stop at Char Dukan for a cup of tea, or walk towards Lal Tibba, one of the area's best-known viewpoints. Its slower pace and forested surroundings make it appealing to travellers who prefer a peaceful break over a packed sightseeing itinerary. AccuWeather's latest dated reading available for Landour was 85 on 6 November 2026, classified as Poor on its air quality scale. 2. Gangtok, Sikkim For those willing to travel further from Kolkata, Gangtok offers a Himalayan alternative. Located at approximately 1,650 metres, the Sikkimese capital combines mountain views with monasteries, local markets, and natural surroundings. For those willing to travel further from Kolkata, Gangtok offers a Himalayan alternative. Photograph: (Travel India) Visitors can explore Rumtek Monastery, walk along MG Marg or take a trip to Tsomgo Lake. The surrounding mountain landscape also offers opportunities to experience Sikkim's local culture and food. On 6 November 2026, Gangtok recorded an AQI of 33 , classified as Good under India's AQI scale. The reading came from the Zero Point GICI monitoring station under the Sikkim State Pollution Control Board. 3. Madikeri, Karnataka Bengaluru residents looking for a change of environment can head to Madikeri in Kodagu, a region known for its coffee plantations, forest patches, and waterfalls. Visitors can explore Abbey Falls, located around eight kilometres from Madikeri, or head to Raja's Seat for views of the surrounding valleys. Coffee estate stays also offer an opportunity to walk through plantations and learn about how coffee is grown. Bengaluru residents looking for a change of environment can head to Madikeri in Kodagu. Photograph: (INIKA Resorts) On 6 November 2026, Madikeri recorded an AQI of 22 , classified as Good. The reading came from the Stuart Hill monitoring station operated by the Karnataka State Pollution Control Board. The station recorded a 24-hour AQI range of 3-28. 4. Chikkamagaluru, Karnataka Known for its coffee-growing landscape, Chikkamagaluru offers another mountain escape for people looking to spend time away from Bengaluru's busy roads. One of its highlights is Mullayanagiri, Karnataka's highest peak. Visitors can also explore Kemmangundi, which is surrounded by forests, mountain streams, and gardens. The surrounding coffee estates provide another way to experience the region. Chikkamagaluru offers another mountain escape for people looking to spend time away from Bengaluru's busy roads. Photograph: (Cozycozy) On 6 November 2026, Chikkamagaluru recorded an AQI of 38 , placing it in the Good category. The reading came from the Kalyana Nagara monitoring station. 5. Coonoor, Tamil Nadu Coonoor, in the Nilgiri Hills, is a peaceful alternative to Ooty for travellers who want to experience the mountains without spending their entire holiday in a busy tourist centre. The hill town is known for its tea-covered slopes and scenic railway journey. Visitors can explore Sim's Park, walk through tea estates or visit viewpoints such as Lamb's Rock and Dolphin's Nose. Coonoor, in the Nilgiri Hills, is a peaceful alternative to Ooty for travellers. Photograph: (Nilgiris Explorers) On 6 November 2026, AccuWeather reported an AQI of 11 for Coonoor, placing it in the Excellent category on its own scale. Can the hills really offer cleaner air? Travelling to the hills can mean spending less time around congested roads and dense urban development, but a lower AQI is never guaranteed. Weather conditions, tourist traffic, construction, and local pollution sources can change readings from one day to another. According to the Central Pollution Control Board, an AQI between 0 and 50 falls in the Good category, while 51 to 100 is considered Satisfactory. It is also important to check which AQI scale a platform uses. India's CPCB index and international indices can have different categories and breakpoints, so their numbers cannot always be compared directly. Before planning a trip , check the latest readings and identify the monitoring station or data source behind them. Choosing accommodation away from busy roads and exploring quieter parts of a destination can also help. The hills cannot promise pollution-free air. But checking the numbers before travelling can help you make a more informed choice about where to spend your next break.

items.description: Καλώς ήρθατε πίσω στο The Spark, τη μηνιαία γιορτή μας για το πώς άνθρωποι σαν εσάς δημιουργούν θετικές αλλαγές, ένα σημαντικό βήμα τη φορά. Εγγραφείτε στο Reasons to be το εβδομαδιαίο ενημερωτικό δελτίο του Cheerful εδώ και θα λαμβάνετε το The Spark στα εισερχόμενά σας στην αρχή κάθε μήνα. Σε αυτό το τεύχος The power of communit…
items.descriptionOriginal: Welcome back to The Spark, our monthly celebration of how people just like you are creating positive change, one meaningful step at a time. The Spark is generously supported by Laura Rice. Sign up to Reasons to be Cheerful’s weekly newsletter here and you’ll get The Spark in your inbox at the start of each month. In this issue The power of community land trusts Cool roofs, cooler homes The perks of intergenerational roommates A community takes back its land In 2019, Nachand Trabue began noticing investors’ “We buy houses” signs all over her corner of Louisville, Kentucky. A historically Black neighborhood since the Civil War, Smoketown has deep roots and a long, proud past — including the city’s first Black library and first Black dentist, and as the birthplace of Muhammed Ali. But increasingly, long-term residents were getting priced out of their own community. For those like Trabue, a fourth-generation resident who remembered Smoketown in its thriving heyday, the change in their community was especially galling. “Because they’re taking away everything that made Smoketown great. They’re buying up the parks, the vacant lots, and putting in houses. There’s nothing for the kids. There’s no enrichment, no activity,” says Theresa Boyd, executive director of Smoketown Community Land Trust. A mural in Smoketown by The Art of Kacy. Credit: Don Sniegowski Trabue had had enough — she started pulling out the investors’ signs, reached out to the city’s land bank to figure out which vacant lots in the neighborhood were held by the city and connected with River City Housing , a local nonprofit home developer, to see how they could work together. At the same time, “the Smoketown Originals started to come together,” says Boyd, referring to a community organization of older residents with deep roots in the neighborhood. “They went to the churches, the community centers, the youth centers.” They started pushing the city to do a housing needs assessment and got in touch with Grounded Solutions , a national nonprofit for affordable housing, to decide whether a community land trust would be a viable option. Community land trusts (CLTs) are grassroots nonprofits that provide long-term affordable housing by buying and developing land on behalf of the community. When selling or renting homes, the CLT retains ownership of the land they’re built on, which makes the homes cheaper and keeps the land itself under community control. Crucially, CLTs also preserve affordability long-term by requiring owners to sell at an affordable price. The first CLTs grew out of the civil rights movement to secure land ownership for Black farmers. Today, they are an increasingly popular way of protecting land from speculators and creating long-term affordable housing, with over 300 CLTs in the US . The CLT’s first houses were recently completed, and more plots have already been chosen. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT In Smoketown, a lot of the initial work focused on explaining what a CLT is and getting the broader community on board. “Communities that have been divested [from] and have been talked to and at versus with, they lose their voice,” says Boyd. “We really had to rally the troops here in the community to be like, ‘You actually have a say in what goes on in your community.’” In 2020 the community and its partner organizations won the city’s Request for Proposals, securing $2.1 million to create a CLT. By 2023 the CLT was formalized and Boyd was brought onboard as the executive director. “I really whipped us into shape administratively and organizationally,” she says. “But most importantly, I went back out into the community and I was like, ‘Okay, this is what you wanted. Now what are we going to do with this land?’” Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Based on a series of surveys, Smoketown CLT built its first seven houses right across the street from where Muhammed Ali threw his first punches under the watchful eye of trainer Fred Stoner, the grandfather of the CLT board president. These houses were recently completed, and the next seven plots have already been chosen. Before starting new developments, the CLT approaches the people living around the plots, says Boyd. “We invite them to the table: Okay, what are your concerns? What are your comments? This is what we are thinking. Is it a viable housing option for your street?” CLTs come in many different shapes, sizes and funding arrangements. In Smoketown, the CLT is funding the construction of the houses, but received the plots of land for free from the city. The land bank has earmarked around 70 plots in the neighborhood for the trust, says Boyd: “We were fortunate that those that came before me had enough gall to go to the city and be like, “Y’all holding all this land and you are absolutely not going to give it to investors. You are going to earmark it for the Community Land Trust.’ And we made them put it in writing.” Mayor Craig Greenberg joined Smoketown CLT to celebrate the completion of the CLT’s first seven homes. Courtesy of Smoketown CLT The city government has been supportive of the CLT, says Boyd, but it would not have happened without the community putting years of work into it. “Louisville’s been around for a really long time, and the people in our community absolutely will hold them to task, and that’s absolutely what they did. They started showing up at the council meetings, the reallocation of funds.” Partnering with experts, like Grounded Solutions, is key to getting a CLT off the ground, as is ensuring that community members see themselves represented in the CLT leadership, says Boyd. “[And] you have to be willing to change and really meet people where they are and not be afraid to make good trouble.” Learn more about Smoketown Community Land Trust here , or get additional information from Grounded Solutions here . Keeping it cool one roof at a time When Tony Chaves noticed how extreme heat and rising air-conditioning costs were affecting his Las Vegas neighborhood, he decided to help solve the problem with a ladder and a bucket of ultra-reflective white paint. As part of the two-person nonprofit Alchemical Opus, Chavez started painting the roofs of Arts District businesses for free, significantly decreasing their indoor temperatures, with one business owner reporting saving $60 to $70 a month on electricity. Coating roofs in white paint is an easy way to lower the temperatures of homes and public buildings. In recent years homeowners across India, Burkina Faso, Mexico and South Pacific have painted their roofs white as part of a global scientific study, with early results indicating substantial cooling. In the U.S., Philadelphia gave 62 households free cool-roof coatings in a 2025 pilot project, while the New York City CoolRoofs program has painted over 12 million square feet of roofs with reflective white paint since 2007. A number of U.S. cities also require cool roofs on new and re-roofed buildings. Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime The science behind the idea is straightforward: White and reflective roofs absorb less solar heat, and applying reflective coatings is the easiest way to transform a roof into a so-called “cool roof,” while also prolonging the life of the roof . The U.S. Department of Energy says cool roofs can reduce annual air-conditioning energy use in single-story buildings by up to 15 percent, while other studies show that painted roofs can lower maximum indoor temperatures by 2.2 to 5.9°F in residential buildings that are not air conditioned. Learn more about cool roofs here . Housing across generations After moving from the countryside to Vienna for university, Lukas Hecke, Manuel Schuler and Marlene Welzl experienced first-hand how difficult it could be to find good housing on a student budget. At the same time, they knew the city was full of elderly people with small pensions and large apartments, who often felt lonely after their children grew up and moved out. In 2015 they started connecting older people with spare rooms to younger people looking for a place to live. It began organically, by word of mouth, and soon grew into the housing platform Wohnbuddy that has carefully matched over 400 people based on their interests and communications over the years. The impact goes beyond private homes. Since 2017, Wohnbuddy has also partnered with senior residences, where students bring new energy through activities, music and social interaction. Learn more about Wohnbuddy here . The post The Spark: When Communities Own the Land, Housing Stays Affordable appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.descriptionOriginal: Northwestern University reports that "over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years." It not only means limited access to local news, but job loss for staff who live in and have long-term relationships with the community. Academic institutions such as Northwestern are working with students to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications focused on serving the community over profit. Students and academic staff work together to provide the journalism for the community while students earn credits or internships. "While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school's building, it operates independently." One journalism school director said, "They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective," she said. "They're trusted in their communities. They know what's going on."

items.descriptionOriginal: Description: She just made history as Los Angeles’ first South Asian mayor-elect! Kerala-born Nithya Raman defeated incumbent Karen Bass with 52.1% of the vote. But her journey to this moment began thousands of miles away. Born in Thrissur, Kerala, Nithya spent her early years in Thiruvananthapuram before moving to the US with her family at around six. After graduating from Harvard in 2003, she returned to India to work with communities often left out of urban development plans. In Delhi, she supported slum residents facing eviction ahead of the 2010 Commonwealth Games. In Chennai, she founded Transparent Chennai, using data mapping to make civic issues in underserved neighbourhoods visible to policymakers. After earning a master’s in urban planning from MIT, she moved to Los Angeles, working on housing and homelessness. In 2020, she entered politics, winning a seat on LA’s City Council. She was re-elected in 2024. Now, she is set to lead the city. She once worked to make overlooked communities heard. Now, she has a city of millions listening. ❤️ #WomenInPolitics #IndianWomen #NithyaRaman #LosAngelesMayor #WomenInPolitics #Kerala #IndianInspiration #Thrissur #InidaninUSA #UrbanPlanning #WomenWhoLead #IndianDiaspora #MadeHistory #TheBetterIndia

items.descriptionOriginal: Happy Eco News Protecting Congo Basin Peatlands Gets a Scientific Boost Reading Time: 3 minutes A major research collection on African tropical peatlands provides new scientific backing for protecting Congo Basin peatlands and strengthens UNEP’s conservation efforts. A major research collection published in September provides new scientific backing for protecting Congo Basin peatlands . The special issue, released in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, brings together studies on the ecology, hydrology, and social dimensions of African tropical peatlands. Much of the research centers on the Cuvette Centrale, the vast peat swamp spanning the Republic of Congo and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Scientists first mapped the full extent of these peatlands in 2017, revealing a wetland larger than England hidden deep in the Congo Basin’s swamp forests. Researchers estimated the area holds roughly 30 billion metric tons of carbon, an amount comparable to about three years of global fossil fuel emissions. That discovery reshaped how researchers think about tropical peatlands’ role in regulating the planet’s carbon cycle. Keeping that carbon locked underground depends entirely on the peat staying wet. Drainage, agricultural conversion, or sustained drought could release large amounts of stored carbon dioxide back into the atmosphere. Protecting Congo Basin peatlands therefore hinges less on stopping any single threat and more on preserving the hydrological conditions that keep the peat intact. The new research collection highlights how much remains unknown about these dynamics. Contributors point to persistent gaps in understanding how the peatlands might respond to future shifts in rainfall, temperature, and land use. Closing those gaps has become a priority for governments and international partners working across the region. International attention around the peatlands has grown steadily since their 2017 discovery. In 2018, the Republic of Congo, the Democratic Republic of Congo, and Indonesia signed a joint declaration committing to protect their peatlands from unregulated development. The agreement built on momentum from the Global Peatlands Initiative, which has pushed peatland protection higher on the global policy agenda. That cooperation extends beyond the three signatory countries themselves. Researchers and policymakers from outside the region have increasingly framed protecting Congo Basin peatlands as a shared international responsibility, given how much global climate stability depends on keeping the carbon in place. Scientific exchange between African, European, and Asian institutions has become a regular feature of that ongoing collaboration. Protecting Congo Basin peatlands has evolved into a shared international responsibility, with the Republic of Congo, DRC, and Indonesia’s 2018 joint declaration and growing scientific collaboration between African, European, and Asian institutions reflecting global recognition that the climate stability of the entire planet depends on keeping this carbon in the ground. Photo courtesy of the UN Environment Programme . Much of the scientific groundwork behind that cooperation comes from research programs such as CongoPeat, led by the University of Leeds. The project has mapped peat extent and carbon stocks across the central Congo Basin while studying how the ecosystem has formed and changed over thousands of years. That evidence base now feeds directly into regional conservation planning. Translating that science into action falls largely to the Congo Basin Landscapes Initiative, a UNEP-led effort working with regional governments and partners. Within that framework, a dedicated peatlands project backed by Germany’s International Climate Initiative is supporting work in the Lac Télé–Lac Tumba landscape. The project represents nearly €15 million in funding between 2022 and 2027. One tool developed under the project models how different development and climate scenarios could affect water levels and carbon storage across the landscape. Results consistently point to the same conclusion: altering drainage patterns carries real risks for the carbon locked in peat. That finding reinforces why protecting Congo Basin peatlands depends so heavily on careful land-use planning. Research led by the University of Leeds shows the peatlands remain mostly intact today, though threats from road building, logging, and resource extraction continue to grow around their edges. Keeping that intact status will require sustained funding and coordination well beyond any single research project or funding cycle. Protecting Congo Basin peatlands adds another layer of evidence to that ongoing effort rather than offering a final answer. Protecting one of the world’s largest carbon stores will continue to depend on scientists, governments, and local communities working from the same shared body of knowledge. For the Congo Basin, that sustained collaboration may matter as much as any single policy or funding commitment. items.descriptionOriginal: Chandigarh's iconic Sukhna Wetland has been officially designated as India's 103rd Ramsar Site. The wetland has been assigned Site Number 2602, placing Chandigarh on the global map of internationally recognised wetlands. On the edge of Chandigarh, where the Shivalik Hills rise towards the Himalayas, Sukhna Lake offers residents more than a stretch of open water. Its banks, surrounding vegetation and adjoining woodland form habitats that sustain wildlife, including birds that travel thousands of kilometres between continents. The lake serves as a feeding, breeding, roosting, and wintering ground for migratory waterbirds. Photograph: (Unpetitprole) Sukhna is a peri-urban reservoir. This means it is a waterbody located within or near an urban area, while still performing important ecological functions. Now, this ecological importance has received international recognition. Four habitats, one interconnected ecosystem A wetland is not simply an expanse of water. Its ecological character depends on the different habitats that exist within and around it, and these habitats allow different forms of wildlife to use the wetland in different ways. Some species depend on the open water, while others use the vegetation along the banks or the surrounding woodland. This diversity is particularly important for birds that use Sukhna as a seasonal stopover. For migratory waterbirds, wetlands are not isolated destinations. They form part of larger geographical routes connecting breeding grounds, feeding areas and wintering habitats. A stop along the Central Asian Flyway Sukhna lies along the Central Asian Flyway , a major migratory route used by birds travelling between their breeding and non-breeding grounds. During these journeys, birds need suitable places to feed, rest and recover before continuing their migration. Wetlands such as Sukhna provide these essential habitats. The lake serves as a feeding, breeding, roosting, and wintering ground for migratory waterbirds. Each of these functions matters at a different stage of a bird's life cycle. Sukhna also supports species with different conservation statuses, highlighting the importance of protecting its habitats. India's Ramsar Site network grows to 103! With Sukhna Lake in Chandigarh and Sauj Jheel in Uttar Pradesh joining the list, India's commitment to wetland conservation continues to grow. These wetlands conserve biodiversity, strengthen water and climate security, and sustain local livelihoods. Their recognition also reinforces the importance of protecting these vital ecosystems for future generations. #AmritDharohar — MoEF&CC (@moefcc) October 15, 2026 Three notable species associated with the wetland include: Common Pochard: Classified as Vulnerable, this diving duck depends on suitable freshwater habitats. Pallas's Fish Eagle: Classified as Endangered, this large raptor is associated with wetland and riverine ecosystems. Black Pond Turtle: Classified as Endangered, this freshwater turtle depends on suitable aquatic environments for its survival. What does the Ramsar designation mean? The Ramsar Convention is an international agreement for the conservation and wise use of wetlands. Named after the Iranian city where it was adopted in 1971, it provides a framework for recognising wetlands that are important at an international level. Being included on the Ramsar List brings international recognition to a wetland's ecological significance and draws attention to the need for its conservation. With Sukhna's inclusion, India's Ramsar network now stands at 103 sites. For Chandigarh, the designation places one of its important urban wetlands within this international conservation framework. Its new status is therefore more than an international listing . It is recognition that even within a planned city, a wetland can remain part of a much larger ecological network, connecting local landscapes with wildlife and migratory routes that extend far beyond national boundaries. Sources: 'India's Ramsar Site tally reaches 103 with addition of Sukhna Wetland (Chandigarh) and Sauj Jheel (UP)' : By PIB Delhi, Published on 15 October 2026 'The Ramsar Sites Criteria-The nine criteria for identifying Wetlands of International Importance' : By Ramsar Convention on Wetlands 'Sukhna Lake-Chandigarh' : Chandigarh Tourism

items.description: Αν κοιτάξετε γύρω σας και σκέφτεστε τους ανθρώπους με τους οποίους αλληλεπιδράτε καθημερινά και θεωρείτε φίλους, πιστεύετε ειλικρινά ότι θα είστε ακόμα κοντά σε πέντε χρόνια; Είτε είναι ο συνάδελφος με τον οποίο γευματίζεις κάθε μέρα, ο γείτονας που μόλις μετακόμισε και τον βλέπεις για ποτά το Σαββατοκύριακο είτε το κορίτσι με το οποίο βγαίνει ο καλύτερος σου φίλος εδώ και ένα χρόνο…
items.descriptionOriginal: If you look around and think of the people you interact with every day that you consider friends, do you honestly think you’ll still be close in five years? Whether it’s the coworker you have lunch with every day, the neighbor who just moved in that you see for drinks on the weekend, or the girl that your best friend has been dating for a year or so, these are all relationships based on proximity, and if that’s gone, will the relationship continue? What is the 5-year-stranger theory? The idea that you’re only close to your friends for about five years or so, and then they slowly drift away, is known as the 5-year-stranger theory. “The framing across the internet is that this drifting apart is a natural evolution of friendship and part of personal growth,” Amanda Burback, a licensed marriage and family therapist and founder of Mellow Therapy in Los Angeles, told Vice . “It’s not a failure of friendship by any means; it’s more the natural evolution of personal growth and personal relationships.” “A lot of that is because friendships are often tied to a shared context of where you are in your life at that moment, whether you’re working the same job, living in the same city or neighborhood, maybe you both recently had children, or both got puppies, whatever it might be,” says Burback. “When the context changes, the friendship can often change with it, not because anyone did anything wrong. It’s just natural growth and different life transitions.” Female friends holding each other. Photo credit: Canva It can be upsetting to think that some of the people you enjoy today may be someone you rarely talk to in a few years. But slowly, the texts stop, and you say, “We gotta hang out and catch up,” but that day never happens. Most of the time, you never know when the last day you spend face-to-face with a good friend will be. But it’s also comforting to know that the true nature of friendship is that most fade, and to appreciate them while they’re around. It’s like “Campfire Theory,” which suggests we are all just sitting by a campfire, and some stop by for a spell to enjoy your warmth and energy, and then move on. Others stay ’til the last ember burns out. Roasting marshmallows over a fire. Photo credit: Canva Is the 5-year-stranger theory real? A social media study by Stockholm University, entitled “Changes in personal relationships: How social contexts affect the emergence and discontinuation of relationships,” found that over seven years, only 48% of a person’s close contacts remained in their network. Only 30% of them still played the same role as a personal friend or practical helper. Interestingly, over the seven years, the size of a person’s network stayed stable, with some people moving in and others moving out. It may be a letdown to realize that many of the people you’re close with today may not be in your inner circle in seven years. The social media trend and study are a wake-up call to be a good steward of your friendships and, if the context changes, to keep in touch and make plans so the friendship doesn’t fade. If you stay in touch with that coworker who got a new job, or your neighbor who moved to another city, you can maintain the friendship; it’s just a little harder when the context isn’t working in your favor. The post Psychologists’ ‘5-year-stranger theory’ is comforting in a world where relationships come and go appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Work, traffic, the price of food and gas— modern life is a lot . We probably all dream of escaping our hectic daily routines on occasion. Just think of the peace a simpler existence might provide. A life far away from endless emails and constant notification pings. But when it comes to the “simple life,” some were more modest than others, like the lonely, ascetic lifestyle of a medieval hermit. Max Miller of the popular YouTube channel Tasting History recently went viral for recreating one particularly humble dish of medieval recluses: fried fava beans and onions. It’s a meal that’s rustic, basic, and surprisingly satisfying . And the hilarious online reactions proved just how ready everyone is to throw in the towel and retreat to the woods. Trading modern stress for medieval beans Miller’s deep dive into historical archives uncovered how some medieval recluses sustained themselves. A note on parchment described how one early hermit survived on just “barley bread and muddy water.” Others enjoyed slightly more comforting vegetable stews, or “pottages.” As for Miller’s 14th-century fried legume recipe, the prep is pretty simple: boil dried fava beans until they burst, and shell the husks. Then toss in chopped onions and minced garlic, and fry everything together in oil. It is the absolute definition of minimalist cooking. Fans flooded the comment sections with pure comedic gold. One viewer joked, “I’m a little upset that Medieval Hermit was not an option provided by my guidance counselor.” Another chimed in, “Some of those fasting meals are appalling, but the one you’re making looks kinda good.” Others considered how this daily meal might affect their relationships. “My wife will force me into my hermitage if I eat a dish of beans and onions,” one fan quipped. As costs rise for everyday households, many followers called the historic repast the ultimate financial warning sign. “This video is a recession indicator,” one top comment read. The bizarre reality of ancient solitude versus today When we picture a modern hermit, we imagine a quiet cottage, a crackling fire, and stacks and stacks of books. The actual reality of a medieval hermit’s existence was far harsher than our cozy digital fantasies. In his video, Miller further reveals that some medieval recluses (many of them monks and nuns) voluntarily agreed to be walled up inside tiny stone cells attached to churches . They lived there permanently with only three small windows to the outside world. Often, they focused on finding ways to demonstrate their willpower, like wearing shirts made from scratchy goat hair. They relied completely on strangers to pass basic meals to them through a slot in the wall. In the 18 th century, hermits oddly became status symbols for rich landowners . Basically, these rich landowners hired them to live on vast estates. Known as “ornamental hermits,” they had to commit to living unwashed in posh gardens as living decorations for party guests. Compared to their extreme discipline, our modern attempts at “unplugging” look pretty luxurious. How often have you struggled to turn off your phone for even a day? Watching someone fry up a simple medieval bean dish offers a fascinating reality check and a reminder that humans have survived tough times with very little for centuries. And that sautéed beans can be delicious. The post Man’s how-to ‘Eat Like a Medieval Hermit’ video has folks starving for the simple life appeared first on Upworthy .

Αλλά τι γίνεται αν επιδιώκουμε το λάθος t…
items.descriptionOriginal: As one of the “inalienable rights” listed in the United States Declaration of Independence, the pursuit of happiness holds a high place in our psyches. In fact, it’s so ingrained in us that we rarely question it. Doesn’t everyone want to be happy? Of course we do. For many, happiness is the ultimate life goal. But what if we’re pursuing the wrong thing? Actor Tom Hiddleston eloquently shared his philosophy on happiness in an episode of SubwayTakes , and the Loki star’s explanation closely aligns with what experts on the topic say. Tom Hiddleston says happiness is overrated and spending your life chasing it can actually make you unhappy "Happiness is overrated. Meaning is underrated. Happiness is like a sunrise or a sunset. Bear with me" "You're there. It's lovely. You're present with it. The sun's rising… pic.twitter.com/ei4qyvfla1 — sara (@saradotxyz) November 3, 2026 ‘Happiness is overrated. Meaning is underrated.’ SubwayTakes asks people to share their five most controversial hot takes, and one of Hiddleston’s was “Happiness is overrated. Meaning is underrated.” “So, happiness is like a sunrise or a sunset. Bear with me…” Hiddleston said. “You’re there. It’s lovely. You’re present with it. The sun’s rising or the sun’s setting, it’s perfect. After 15 minutes, the moment is over, and it’s gone. Trying to sustain it is impossible because it’s over. And a life spent chasing the permanence of that feeling, I think, will make you unhappy because you can’t hold onto it. The moment you try to hold onto it, it slips through your fingers and is lost.” Hiddleston shared that meaning, on the other hand, is a whole different story. “Meaning is a structure that only you create in your own life,” he said, “an architecture with your own particular spiritual fingerprint, whereby if you’re going through a hard time, if you’re going through challenge, struggle, obstacles, suffering, or pain, only you know why you’re going through it.” Doing something hard for the sake of your kids, or your mom, or your future is “bearable because you know what it means,” he shared. “And meaning—this is the take—meaning yields joy. Joy is deeper than happiness.” View this post on Instagram A happiness expert’s take Dr. Arthur C. Brooks is one of the foremost experts on this topic, having made happiness the focus of much of his research and multiple books. According to Brooks, meaning doesn’t replace happiness; it is one of its three pillars—and the one most often neglected. “Happiness rests on three pillars: enjoyment, satisfaction, and meaning,” Brooks shared in a LinkedIn post. “Today, meaning is collapsing, especially for the young, because we’ve neglected the part of the brain that asks ‘why.'” Brooks explains that modern life is so focused on the “how” and “what” questions that many people rarely even access the part of their brain that asks “Why?” “This is a crisis,” he says. Brooks explains that we need to ask the big, complex “why” questions like, “Why am I alive?” and “Why would I be willing to give my life?” in order to delve into the pillar of meaning that leads to happiness. Psychologists have defined meaning as a combination of coherence (things happen for a reason), purpose (direction in life), and significance (your life matters). We can make do without enjoyment for a while, and even with little satisfaction. But if we lack meaning—which takes a… — Dr. Arthur Brooks (@arthurbrooks) September 12, 2024 How to explore meaning that leads to happiness Here are the elements of meaning, according to Brooks, and the questions that help us find it: Coherence: Why do things happen the way they do? (Exploring this question helps life make sense, rather than chalking events up to randomness or chaos.) Purpose: What are my goals, and why am I moving in this direction? (This question helps give us a trajectory, so we’re moving toward something rather than flailing about aimlessly.) Significance: Why does it matter? (This question helps us understand how our life makes a positive difference to others and the world.) View this post on Instagram Of course, that’s simply an ingredients list for meaning, not the entire recipe. Brooks has lots of tips for finding meaning, including one that’s often overlooked: experiencing beauty. Seeing something so beautiful that it makes you want to cry, and you can’t find the words to describe it, is one way to tap into the “why” part of the brain. That might be a beautiful piece of music or a gorgeous vista. Or it might be moral beauty: someone who touches your soul with their acts of compassion or kindness. You can find more from Dr. Brooks on the science of happiness on his website , and see more of Tom Hiddleston’s thoughtful takes in the full SubwayTakes episode here: The post Tom Hiddleston eloquently explained why happiness is overrated. Experts say he’s (mostly) right. appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Hayden Christensen, who played Anakin Skywalker in the Star Wars prequels , was once on the phone at home, waiting for a friend, when he heard the front door open. Then he heard footsteps heading up the stairs. He assumed his friend was just goofing around, so he played along , doing what he called “a sort of do-si-do” with the visitor around his walk-around fireplace, then sat back down and kept talking on the phone. Eventually, he got up to see what his friend was doing. It wasn’t his friend. “I’m like, is this a delivery guy?” Christensen said. “And I look and I’m like, this is all my stuff.” Hayden Christensen during the premiere of Star Wars Episode III in May 2005 in Berlin. Photo credit: MarcoKraus via Wikimedia Commons Christensen told the story on Oct. 30 at his L.A. Comic Con panel , when the moderator asked about the strangest fan encounter of his career, according to The Nerd Wire , which reported from the room. It turned out the man knew exactly whose house he was in. Christensen said the intruder immediately apologized, returned what he’d taken, and said he was broke and just trying to scrape together enough cash to get home. So Christensen offered to cover it, saying if the man came back the next day, he’d drive him to the train station and pay for his ticket. And when the man said he’d never land a job dressed the way he was, Christensen brought him upstairs and outfitted him with clothes and shoes. But he never showed up for the ride. Christensen ended the story with a message for the room. “Please don’t try to burglarize my house again,” he said. “I’ve got great security cameras.” The post Star Wars’ Hayden Christensen caught a burglar with an armful of his stuff. Then the burglar recognized him. appeared first on Upworthy .

Αυτό είναι το wo…
items.descriptionOriginal: Picture a small workshop in Goa, barely large enough to turn around in. A furnace glows in one corner, the air thick with heat and the faint metallic smell of melting gold. An artisan bends over a workbench, a single sharpened wire in hand, and begins to carve a name into a ring, stroke by careful stroke, with no machine to help him. This is the world Prachi Shirodkar spent months filming for her documentary Bhaangar Kalakusar Karigiri , a world she knew intimately because her own father and grandfather had once worked in it. The 28-year-old directed, shot and narrated the documentary , handling the filming herself, while her father wrote the script and her partner edited the film. 'Lockdown changed all my plans' Shirodkar was one year into a B.Arch degree in 2020 when the country went into lockdown. Lockdown in 2020 prompted Prachi Shirodkar to leave architecture behind and discover her calling in storytelling. With classes paused and the world outside shut down, she found herself alone with her thoughts for the first time in years. "When you're by yourself, that's when you really get to know yourself," she says of that period. What she discovered was that design had never been the thing pulling at her . Storytelling was, and always had been. She had grown up around theatre and acting, but with no one in her family from the film or media industry, architecture had felt like the safer, more familiar choice after school. The lockdown gave her room to reconsider, and she switched to mass communication instead. "This was my element," she tells The Better India. "I am myself. I know what I'm doing, and I love it." Her father's script, her camera & a story rooted in Goa For her final-year project, Shirodkar turned the camera on the goldsmiths she had grown up watching at work. "I'm not trying to represent the community here; it's about their art and their skill," she says of her intention. With no filmmaking experience or fixed schedule, Shirodkar began documenting artisans she had known since childhood. Photograph: (Still from the film) She also made a deliberate choice to include women artisans in the film. "It's not just men who do this anymore," she says. Making the film in Konkani was never really a decision at all. "I am Goan, this is happening in Goa, and Konkani is my mother tongue. I didn't have to think twice," she says, noting that even within the language, the dialects of Mapsa, Pernem and Margao carry their own small differences. Her father, who had worked in the trade himself, wrote the film's script in that specific vocabulary, giving her a foundation to build the film around. Her father's experience in goldsmithing shaped the documentary's Konkani script, preserving the trade's vocabulary and cultural roots. The project almost didn't happen. It began as a college group assignment that fell through when the group arrangement did not work out, and Shirodkar shelved it, intending to return to it only after graduation. It was her partner, Mario Pimenta, who convinced her to pick it back up. "It was his idea. I'm grateful he pushed for it," she says. He went on to edit the film while she handled the filming, direction and narration herself, despite having never operated a camera before. There was no fixed shoot schedule and barely any budget. "Whatever I had in hand was what mattered," she says of how she funded it. Shoots depended entirely on when her subjects, many of them relatives and family friends she had known for years, happened to be free. A goldsmith engraving an entire name with a slender wire revealed the remarkable precision behind the traditional craft. This meant filming in scattered bursts across several weeks rather than in one continuous run. Piecing together a coherent narrative from those fragments was one of the hardest parts of the process. "I kept asking myself whether I had the flow right or was missing something," she recalls. One moment stayed with her long after the shoot ended: a craftsman engraving a name into gold with nothing but a slim metal wire. "It doesn't even look like a knife; it looks like a wire," she says. "He carved the entire name using just that. Our hands are so skilled." 'You have a camera, you have a story' The film's festival run began with rejections. Then came an unexpected first selection at Jackson Doc Fest in Tennessee, USA, followed by screenings in Kerala at the International Folklore Film Festival and a selection for the International Cultural Journal Award in Uzhhorod, Ukraine. It also won Best Documentary at the Miseentage Indian Film Awards, and Shirodkar was recently conferred a Young Achievers Award by Rotary International for her contribution to culture. "They just called out my name, and I was genuinely taken aback," she says of the moment. Shirodkar filmed the artisans herself, while her partner Mario Pimenta edited the footage into a cohesive story of Goa's goldsmithing tradition. She now works as an assistant director in Mumbai, and the scale of commercial production has reshaped how she thinks about her own filmmaking. "What you learn in theory is so different from what happens in practice," she says, adding that if she made the film again today, she would write a fuller script and bring in a dedicated cinematographer rather than shoot it herself. Her advice to other young filmmakers starting out without money or a team is blunt and repeated often in conversation: find people you trust, however small the crew. "If you have the right people with you, everything will fall into place," she says. Do not let the absence of a budget stop you from starting. Now an assistant director in Mumbai, Shirodkar urges young filmmakers to begin with the stories closest to home. "There are filmmakers who have made it happen with very little money, and they've done so well," she says. "You have a camera, you have a story. Just go shoot it." And look close to home first, she adds, because the most powerful subjects are often the ones already around you. "Start from where you belong, and then go step by step."

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Κάθε πρωί στον καταυλισμό στο Teknaf, στο Μπαγκλαντές, ο Mohammed Saber ανεβαίνει στην οροφή του σπιτιού της οικογένειάς του από μπαμπού και μουσαμά και τοποθετεί ένα ενιαίο ορθογώνιο ηλιακό πάνελ. Το έκανε αυτό για έξι χρόνια, από τότε που η οικογένειά του διέφυγε από την καταστολή των Ροχίνγκια από τον στρατό της Μιανμάρ το 2017. «Μπορούμε τώρα να χρεώσουμε…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM Every morning in the camp at Teknaf, Bangladesh, Mohammed Saber climbs to the roof of his family’s bamboo-and-tarpaulin home and sets out a single rectangular solar panel. He has done this for six years, since his family fled the Myanmar military’s crackdown on the Rohingya people in 2017. “We can now charge our phones, cook with light, children can study at night and use fans during the hot season,” says Saber, 35. A small panel on a makeshift roof, and an entire household runs on it. The same thing is happening in camps and disaster zones around the world. Solar has been edging into humanitarian response for years; what’s shifted is how seriously organizations are taking it, less as an experiment and more as something people actually need. From lanterns to cook stoves The range of what “solar kit” means is wider than it might sound. Sarah Rosenberg-Jansen , a research fellow at the Stockholm Environment Institute , describes the category as spanning solar lanterns, torches, and heating pads to full solar home systems and electric cook stoves . The common thread is portability and independence from the grid, which matters most when infrastructure is gone and things are moving fast. “In emergency situations , solar kits can be deployed immediately,” she says. That’s playing out across multiple places at once. In Karachi, Doctors Without Borders runs a tuberculosis clinic on solar power. In South Sudan’s Renk County , the UN migration agency installed solar-powered water filtration for families displaced by the war in neighboring Sudan. When Nepal’s floods killed 1,455 people and left 5,285 missing in August, local and international organizations distributed solar kits to survivors cut off from the grid. In Ukraine, a nonprofit called Hope For Ukraine has provided kits to thousands of families living through a war, including older residents who adapted without trouble. “We have grandmas and grandpas who are around 75 to 80 years old receiving kits,” says CEO Yuriy Boyechko. “It’s just a matter of plug and play.” Why costs finally shifted Solar panels don’t carry the same price volatility as fossil fuels, which are expensive and difficult to transport into disaster zones under ordinary circumstances and near-impossible when infrastructure has been destroyed. Only a few decades ago, solar was a luxury technology. Mass manufacturing and steady advances in efficiency changed that, and the price drop put solar kits within reach of humanitarian budgets in ways they weren’t before. Funding cuts and the waiting list What’s slowing things down now isn’t the technology. Aid organizations have long-running contracts built around diesel generators, and switching to solar means trusting new equipment, building new distribution chains, and sometimes doing that in genuinely hazardous conditions. Mark Gibson of the Global Platform for Action , a group promoting clean energy access, notes that the transition has been complicated for organizations with established logistics in place. Cuts to international donor funding have made it harder. Aimee Jenks, a program leader at GPA, was direct: “Much of the technical expertise in the humanitarian sector on energy has been cut. That’s now retracting a lot of progress.” Hope For Ukraine’s own numbers show how stretched the system is. By the end of 2026, the organization expects to have distributed more than 3,200 solar kits, a number that took two years to reach because of funding. “We have a waiting list of about 20,000 families,” Boyechko says. “We just cannot keep up with demand.” For Saber, the gap between what’s available and what people have isn’t an abstraction. His family has had their panel for six years, long enough to know exactly what changed. “It’s improved my family’s life,” he says. Did this solution stand out? items.descriptionOriginal: The U.K.’s first “Flower Pharmacy” opened its doors last month — prescribing bouquets instead of medicine to those in need of a mood boost. The one-off experience in London was designed to encourage people to think differently about flowers, showing how they can play a role in everyday well-being rather than just being reserved for birthdays, anniversaries, and other special occasions. It was created in partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland and chartered horticulturist, TV gardener, and author David Domoney. Guests were matched with blooms tailored to their mood before leaving with a bouquet recommended to lift, calm, or energize them. For example, yellow flowers, including sunflowers, roses, freesias, and snapdragons, were prescribed to boost happiness, while calming bouquets featured blue and green blooms like hydrangeas, delphiniums, and chrysanthemums. For those who needed a dose of energy, there were also vibrant orange, red, and pink flowers. Courtesy of SWNS The event came as a poll of 2,000 British adults found 37% struggle when daylight saving time ends, with 29% admitting the time change leaves them feeling glum. Discussing the partnership with Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, which commissioned the research and the pop-up, Domoney said: “There’s something incredibly uplifting about flowers, and research has shown that they can have a positive effect on our mood and emotional well-being. From the cheerful yellows of sunflowers and freesias to the calming tones of blues and greens, color can influence how we experience the spaces around us.” “We often associate flowers with special occasions, but there’s no reason we shouldn’t enjoy their beauty and the benefits of having them around us in everyday life,” he continued. “Sometimes, it’s the simplest connections with nature that can make a real difference to how we feel.” Courtesy of SWNS The survey also found that around a third of respondents spend more time indoors following the clock change, while 28% find the darker evenings difficult and 22% experience lower energy levels. The good news? There are plenty of ways to lift that low mood, like listening to music, reading a book, exercising, spending time in nature and, yes, buying flowers. While just 9% of people said they regularly treat themselves to blooms, the emotional response to receiving them is clear — half said they feel happy after being presented with a bouquet, 45% grateful, 34% joyful, and 24% comforted. Courtesy of SWNS Monique Kemperman, horticulture expert for Plants and Flowers Foundation Holland, said: “As the days become shorter and darker, small acts of self-care can make a real difference, and flowers are a simple way to bring color, joy, and positivity into everyday life.” “Our research shows just how much of an emotional impact they can have, yet many people still reserve them for somebody else or a special occasion,” she added. “The Flower Pharmacy is about encouraging people to see flowers as an everyday well-being boost rather than a treat.” This article was originally written by Jasmine Lenthall for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Υπάρχει ένα συγκεκριμένο είδος κινήτρου που εμφανίζεται στις γιορτές. Σκέφτεσαι: φέτος, θα κάνω κάτι. Φαντάζεσαι τον εαυτό σου σε μια ποδιά σε μια σούπα και νιώθεις ωραία. Το πρόβλημα είναι ότι πολλοί άλλοι άνθρωποι απεικονίζουν το ίδιο πράγμα την ίδια στιγμή. Οι περισσότερες τράπεζες τροφίμων και κιτ σούπας…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM There’s a particular kind of motivation that kicks in around the holidays. You think: this year, I’m going to do something. You picture yourself in an apron at a soup kitchen, and it feels good. The problem is that a lot of other people are picturing the same thing at the same time. Most food banks and soup kitchens see volunteer demand spike around Thanksgiving , sometimes to the point where they have more help than they can use on that one day. If you want your time to count, a little strategy goes a long way. The good news: there are 17 solid options below, and several of them work whether you have four hours, four minutes, or no desire to leave your couch. National organizations with locations near you These programs operate across all 50 states, so wherever you are, there’s likely a chapter close enough to walk in. Feeding America Feeding America runs the largest hunger-relief network in the country. If you want to volunteer at a food bank on Thanksgiving, call ahead first. Holiday demand often fills slots fast, and some locations redirect walk-ins toward future dates when the need is more consistent. Meals on Wheels Meals on Wheels delivers hot meals to seniors who can’t get out on their own. The flexibility here is part of the appeal: you can sign up for a single delivery route or build it into a regular habit. The Salvation Army The Salvation Army works across a wide range of needs, from veterans to abuse survivors to people experiencing homelessness. There’s almost always something useful you can do, even on short notice. Operation Turkey Operation Turkey runs a tightly organized four-hour shift from 8 a.m. to noon, packing meals for homeless individuals. If you want a defined commitment with a clear end time, this is a good fit. Feed My Starving Children Feed My Starving Children packs meals at permanent sites in Arizona, Illinois, Minnesota, and Texas. It runs on a reservation system, so sign up before the week of. Toys for Tots Toys for Tots runs its drives through December, so Thanksgiving week is peak season. Volunteer slots exist for collection drives, not just drop-offs. Goodwill Goodwill often looks for people who can share a professional skill, not just sort donations. If you have a background in workforce development, finance, or career coaching, that’s where you’d fit in. United Way United Way sponsors a range of community initiatives, including garden planting, literacy programs, and neighborhood projects. What’s available depends on your city, so look up your local chapter. Local options that don’t require a national signup Soup kitchens and community meal programs often run on the same skeleton crew year after year. A call a week ahead is usually all it takes. Animal shelters are another option, especially if you’re better with dogs than crowds. Staff still work on Thanksgiving, and extra hands for walks or socialization are usually welcome. If you’re up for something more active, turkey trots are 5K races held in communities across the country on Thanksgiving morning, with proceeds going to local charities. You walk or run, and the entry fee does the work. The National Park Service also coordinates trail maintenance and cleanup projects throughout the fall. Check the volunteer page for your nearest park. If you can’t leave the house Gift-a-Family Gift-a-Family lets you sponsor a family through their holiday wishlist. The sign-up deadline is November 30, so there’s still time. Homefront America Homefront America directs donations toward grocery and turkey vouchers for military families. Support Our Troops Support Our Troops coordinates handwritten letters to deployed service members. It takes about ten minutes and goes a long way. One thing to know before you go Holiday volunteering is genuinely good, but the reality is that organizations often need year-round help. Of course, showing up once during the holidays could be the gateway to showing up regularly. If you get redirected on Thanksgiving Day because a food bank is at capacity, ask when they need people most. Often the answer is right after the holiday rush! Did this solution stand out? Share it with a friend or support our mission by becoming an Emissary . The post The best places to volunteer this Thanksgiving: 17 options for every schedule first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.title: Η Gen Xers μοιράζεται πώς ήταν να μεγαλώνεις από γονείς Silent Generation αντί για Boomers
